title: Animal allergies: recognising exposure and making a practical plan
intro: An animal allergy is an immune reaction to proteins associated with an animal, including proteins in skin flakes, saliva or urine. Hair can carry these substances, but hair itself is not the whole explanation. Cats, dogs and other animals can trigger symptoms. A new rash or cough around a pet still needs assessment because dust, pollen and other exposures may also be involved.

sections.heading: Look for patterns without deliberately provoking symptoms
paragraphs: Sneezing, a blocked or runny nose, itchy eyes and skin symptoms can occur after exposure. Coughing, wheezing or chest tightness may signal involvement of the airways. Allergens can travel on clothing and remain in furnishings, so symptoms may occur where no animal is currently present. Write down places, timing and breathing symptoms; do not test your theory by deliberately increasing contact, particularly if previous exposure affected breathing.

sections.heading: Use testing in the context of your history
paragraphs: A clinician can assess whether the history fits allergy and whether asthma needs investigation. Skin-prick testing or a blood test for specific antibodies may help identify sensitisation. A positive result does not alone prove that the animal explains every symptom. Tell the testing service about medicines you use and follow its preparation instructions rather than stopping treatment yourself. Bring information about other possible triggers and whether symptoms also occur away from animals.

sections.heading: Understand what hypoallergenic claims cannot promise
paragraphs: Hairless animals and breeds advertised as hypoallergenic can still produce allergens. Individual reactions vary, and choosing a short-haired breed does not guarantee safety. Do not rely on a brief symptom-free visit as proof that living with an animal will be problem-free. Discuss the level of risk and the household's needs before making a major decision, especially when a child or someone with asthma is affected.

sections.heading: Discuss realistic ways to reduce exposure
paragraphs: Depending on circumstances, the plan may include avoiding animal contact, keeping animals out of the bedroom, reducing dust-collecting furnishings and suitable cleaning or filtration. These measures may lower exposure but cannot guarantee symptom control. Allergens can persist after an animal leaves, and restricting it to one room does not contain every particle. Work through affordable, sustainable changes with the household and clinician rather than assuming an expensive device or a single cleaning session will solve the problem.

sections.heading: Match treatment and urgency to the symptoms
paragraphs: Antihistamines, appropriate nasal sprays or eye treatments may be discussed for relevant symptoms. Asthma requires its own assessment and treatment plan; a tablet for sneezing is not a substitute for managing breathing problems. Specialist immunotherapy may be considered in selected cases, with discussion of evidence, risks and commitment. Seek medical advice for repeated wheezing or night-time cough. Severe breathing difficulty, difficulty speaking because of breathlessness, or tongue or throat swelling requires emergency help.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: investigating a household change
examples.text: A family notices a child's cough after adopting a cat. They arrange assessment and describe the timing, wheezing and bedroom environment. They ask whether asthma and other allergens need consideration rather than assuming either that the cat is definitely responsible or that a short coat makes it harmless.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: planning a visit
examples.text: Someone with diagnosed animal allergy asks a relative about pets before an overnight visit. They discuss alternative accommodation and their existing treatment plan with a professional when needed. They do not deliberately spend time with the animal to see how severe the reaction becomes.

Do my coughing or wheezing symptoms need an asthma assessment?
